## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes field procedures for conducting vegetation transect
surveys using three common methods: line-point intercept (LPI), line
intercept (LI), and quadrat (cover class) sampling. These methods
quantify plant species composition, percent cover, and community
structure across field sites and form the basis for vegetation
monitoring, ecological assessment, and restoration evaluation
[@bonham2013; @mueller-dombois1974; @kent2012].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Terrestrial vegetation surveys at all EA Program
  field sites, including the Bernard Field Station, Pomona College
  Farm, the Pit, restoration sites, and photovoltaic panel study areas
- **Does not apply to:** Aquatic or submerged vegetation surveys;
  tree-only forest inventory (DBH-based methods; see
  [SOP-F604](SOP-F604-tree-dbh-forest-inventory.qmd)); remote sensing
  vegetation analysis
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## 3. Definitions

- **Percent cover:** The proportion of the ground surface covered by
  the vertical projection of the aerial parts of a plant species,
  expressed as a percentage. Cover is the standard metric for
  characterizing non-woody vegetation communities because it
  integrates plant size and density into a single measure
  [@bonham2013].
- **Line-point intercept (LPI):** A method that estimates cover by
  recording what a vertically lowered pin contacts at fixed intervals
  along a transect. Originally described by @levy1933, LPI produces
  objective, repeatable cover estimates with minimal observer bias
  [@herrick2005].
- **Line intercept (LI):** A method that measures the length of
  transect tape intercepted by the canopy of each species. Best
  suited for shrubs and other plants with clearly defined canopy
  boundaries.
- **Quadrat:** A fixed-area frame (typically 1 m x 1 m) within which
  percent cover is visually estimated for each species. Visual
  estimation introduces more observer subjectivity than point-based
  methods but permits rapid assessment and better detection of rare
  species [@daubenmire1959; @godinez-alvarez2009].
- **Daubenmire cover class:** A categorical scale for estimating cover
  within quadrats: 1 (0--5%), 2 (5--25%), 3 (25--50%), 4 (50--75%),
  5 (75--95%), 6 (95--100%). The midpoint of each class is used in
  calculations [@daubenmire1959].
- **Top hit / lower hit:** In LPI, the "top hit" is the first species
  the pin contacts as it descends through the canopy; subsequent
  contacts with other species or canopy layers are "lower hits."
  Recording both allows multi-layer canopy analysis.
- **Species richness:** The total number of species recorded in a
  defined area. Richness is strongly influenced by plot size and
  sampling effort [@wilson2012].
- **Voucher specimen:** A pressed, dried, and identified plant
  specimen archived for verification of field identifications. See
  Section 9.
- **Basal cover:** The proportion of ground surface occupied by the
  base (stem or root crown) of a plant, as distinct from foliar
  cover. Basal cover is more stable than foliar cover across seasons
  and is sometimes used for perennial grass monitoring [@herrick2005].


## 4. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve survey design, ensure training compliance       |
| Field Lead        | Coordinate logistics, assign transect locations         |
| Trained Personnel | Conduct surveys, record data, collect voucher specimens |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent surveying          |


## 5. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Biological:** Poison oak, stinging nettle, ticks, snakes, bees
  (all common at local field sites)
- **Physical:** Uneven terrain, heat exposure, sharp stakes and rebar
- **Allergenic:** Pollen exposure during peak growing season
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Long pants (required in areas with poison oak or ticks)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (when handling unknown plants)
- [ ] Tick repellent (DEET or permethrin-treated clothing)

### Required Training

- [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)


## 6. Summary of Methods

Three survey methods are covered in this SOP. Select the method that
best fits your vegetation type and research objectives
[@elzinga1998; @herrick2005].

| Method | Best For | Accuracy | Speed | Observer Bias |
|:-------|:---------|:---------|:------|:--------------|
| **Line-point intercept** | Grasslands, herbaceous communities | High | Moderate | Low |
| **Line intercept** | Shrublands, plants with dense canopies >1 m | High | Slow | Low |
| **Quadrat (cover class)** | Mixed communities, rapid assessment, rare species detection | Moderate | Fast | Moderate |

::: {.callout-tip}
### Choosing a Method
For most EA Program projects in southern California grasslands and
shrublands, **line-point intercept** is the default method because it
minimizes observer bias in cover estimation [@herrick2005;
@godinez-alvarez2009]. Use **quadrats** when rare species detection
is important or when rapid assessment is needed, recognizing that
visual cover estimation varies significantly among observers even
after training [@bonham2013]. Use **line intercept** for
shrub-dominated communities where canopy boundaries are distinct.
When a study spans multiple years, method consistency across years is
more important than selecting the "best" method in any given year
[@symstad2008].
:::


## 7. Required Materials

### Field Equipment

| Item                          | Notes                                          |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|
| 50 m measuring tape           | Fiberglass preferred (doesn't stretch)         |
| Chaining pins or rebar stakes | For anchoring transect endpoints               |
| Pin flags                     | For marking transect start/end and quadrat locations |
| Sampling pin or rod           | Thin metal rod (~3 mm diameter) for point intercept |
| 1 m x 1 m quadrat frame      | PVC or metal; for cover class method           |
| Compass                       | For establishing transect bearings              |
| GPS unit or smartphone        | For recording transect coordinates              |
| Field data sheets             | Printed from Appendix A                        |
| Clipboard and pencils         | Mechanical pencils work well in the field      |
| Plant identification guides   | Regional flora; Jepson Manual for California [@baldwin2012] |
| Camera                        | For photo documentation at each transect       |
| Collection bags and plant press | For voucher specimens of unknown species      |
| Flagging tape                 | For temporary marking                          |


## 8. Estimated Time

| Task                        | Time                                           |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|
| Site preparation and transect setup | 15--30 minutes per transect              |
| Line-point intercept survey | 30--60 minutes per 50 m transect               |
| Line intercept survey       | 45--90 minutes per 50 m transect               |
| Quadrat survey              | 10--15 minutes per quadrat                     |
| Data entry and QC           | 30 minutes per transect (post-field)           |


## 9. Procedure

### 9.1 Survey Timing

Conduct vegetation surveys during the peak growing season for the
target community. In southern California:

- **Grasslands and annual forbs:** March through May
- **Coastal sage scrub:** April through June
- **Riparian:** June through August

Consistency in timing across years is essential for detecting temporal
changes [@symstad2008]. Surveys conducted outside the peak window
will underestimate cover for deciduous and annual species.

### 9.2 Transect Layout

1. Determine transect locations using the project sampling design
   (random, stratified random, or systematic placement within habitat
   zones). The choice of sampling design affects the inferences that
   can be drawn from the data; random or stratified random designs
   support unbiased estimation of population-level cover, while
   systematic designs maximize spatial coverage but can coincide with
   periodic landscape features [@kent2012].
2. Navigate to the starting point and record GPS coordinates
3. Establish the transect bearing using a compass (typically
   perpendicular to environmental gradients, e.g., slope, moisture,
   or distance from structures)
4. Anchor the 0 m end of the measuring tape with a chaining pin
5. Walk out the tape to the desired length (typically 50 m), keeping
   it taut and as straight as possible
6. Anchor the far end with a second chaining pin
7. Photograph the transect from both ends

::: {.callout-note}
### Permanent Transects
For long-term monitoring, mark transect endpoints with permanent
markers (capped rebar driven flush with the ground, GPS coordinates
recorded to sub-meter accuracy). Take a compass bearing and distance
to at least two nearby permanent features for relocation.
:::

### 9.3 Method A: Line-Point Intercept

This method estimates percent cover by recording what a vertical
sampling pin contacts at regular intervals along the transect. The
method was originally developed by @levy1933 for pasture analysis
and has since become the standard for rangeland and grassland
monitoring [@herrick2005].

1. Begin at the 0 m end of the transect; always work from the same
   side of the tape
2. At each sampling point (every 0.5 m or 1 m, depending on project
   design), lower the sampling pin vertically through the vegetation
   canopy directly over the tape
3. Record each plant species the pin contacts as it descends from the
   canopy to the ground (**top hit** is the first species contacted;
   record all species for multi-layer canopies)
4. If the pin does not contact any vegetation, record the ground
   surface type: bare soil, litter, rock, moss/lichen, or other
5. Record the height (cm) of the tallest species contacted at each
   point
6. Advance to the next sampling point and repeat

::: {.callout-important}
### Pin Angle Matters
The pin must be lowered vertically (plumb). Tilting the pin even
slightly increases the probability of contacting vegetation and
inflates cover estimates. Some protocols use a pin guide or frame
to enforce verticality.
:::

**Calculations:**

$$
\text{Percent cover for species } i = \frac{\text{Number of hits for species } i}{\text{Total number of sampling points}} \times 100
$$

Total cover may exceed 100% when canopy layers overlap. The number
of sampling points required depends on the diversity and patchiness
of the vegetation; 100 points per 50 m transect (0.5 m interval) is
standard for diverse grasslands, while 50 points (1 m interval) may
suffice in low-diversity or homogeneous stands [@elzinga1998].

### 9.4 Method B: Line Intercept

This method measures the length of transect tape intercepted by each
plant species. Best suited for shrubs and plants with distinct canopy
boundaries [@bonham2013].

1. Begin at the 0 m end of the transect
2. Walk slowly along the tape, noting where each plant canopy begins
   and ends (intercepts the tape)
3. Record the species, the start point (cm), and the end point (cm)
   on the data sheet
4. If a gap occurs within a single plant's canopy that is longer than
   the canopy width on either side, treat it as two separate
   intercepts
5. Record gaps between plants as the appropriate ground cover type

**Calculations:**

$$
\text{Percent cover for species } i = \frac{\sum \text{intercept lengths for species } i}{\text{Total transect length}} \times 100
$$

### 9.5 Method C: Quadrat (Cover Class)

This method uses visual estimates of cover within fixed-area plots
placed at intervals along the transect [@daubenmire1959].

1. Place quadrats at predetermined intervals along the transect (e.g.,
   every 5 m or 10 m), or at random distances
2. Ensure enough distance between quadrats for them to be independent
   sampling units (typically at least 5 m apart)
3. For each quadrat, identify every plant species present
4. Estimate percent cover for each species using the modified
   Daubenmire cover classes:

| Class | Cover Range | Midpoint |
|:------|:------------|:---------|
| 1     | 0--5%       | 2.5%     |
| 2     | 5--25%      | 15%      |
| 3     | 25--50%     | 37.5%    |
| 4     | 50--75%     | 62.5%    |
| 5     | 75--95%     | 85%      |
| 6     | 95--100%    | 97.5%    |

5. Also record percent cover of bare ground, litter, and rock
6. Note the maximum vegetation height (cm) in each quadrat
7. Photograph each quadrat from directly above

Visual estimation of cover is inherently subjective and sensitive to
observer experience, viewing angle, and vegetation height; training
with known-cover reference images or calibration frames improves
consistency but does not eliminate inter-observer variability
[@godinez-alvarez2009; @bonham2013].


## 10. Voucher Specimens

When a plant cannot be identified in the field:

1. Collect a representative sample including leaves, stems, and
   flowers or fruit if available
2. Place in a labeled collection bag (site, transect, date, collector)
3. Press specimens the same day
4. Identify in the lab using the Jepson Manual [@baldwin2012] or other
   regional flora
5. Update the data sheet with the confirmed identification


## 11. Quality Control

- Two observers should independently estimate cover for at least 10%
  of quadrats to assess observer agreement. Inter-observer variability
  in cover estimation is the largest source of error in quadrat-based
  surveys; training reduces but does not eliminate this bias
  [@elzinga1998; @bonham2013].
- For LPI surveys, duplicate readings at 10% of points should agree
  on species identity for at least 90% of hits. Disagreements on
  ground cover type (e.g., litter vs. bare soil) are most common and
  should be resolved by applying consistent definitions.
- Photograph each transect and quadrat for archival verification
- Review data sheets in the field before leaving the site (check for
  missing entries, illegible writing, and species code consistency)
- Enter data within 48 hours of collection
- Maintain a species list with standardized codes used across all
  surveys


## 12. Data Management

### 12.1 Field Data Sheets

Use the data sheets in Appendix A. Record in pencil (ink smears when
wet). Use Rite in the Rain paper if available.

### 12.2 Data Entry

Enter data into the project spreadsheet or database within 48 hours.
Each row should represent one observation (one point, one intercept,
or one quadrat-species combination). Required fields:

- Date, site, transect ID, observer
- Method (LPI, LI, or Quadrat)
- Point/interval/quadrat number
- Species (use standardized 6-letter codes: first 3 letters of genus +
  first 3 of species, e.g., BRODIA for *Bromus diandrus*)
- Cover value or hit/no-hit
- Height (cm)
- Ground cover type (if applicable)


## 13. Waste and Site Impact

- Remove all flagging tape, pin flags, and temporary markers after the
  survey
- Do not trample vegetation outside the immediate transect corridor
- Leave permanent markers flush with the ground to avoid hazards to
  people and wildlife
- Pack out all trash and supplies

## 15. Training Record

Before conducting vegetation surveys independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)
   in full
2. Demonstrate familiarity with at least 20 common species at the
   study site
3. Participate in a supervised survey using each method to be employed
4. Demonstrate acceptable inter-observer agreement on cover estimates
   (within one cover class for quadrats, or within 5% for line-point
   intercept)
5. Be signed off by the field lead or PI
